Reverence is a feeling — a deep, solemn mixture of respect, awe, and admiration that you feel toward something or someone you consider truly great, sacred, or worthy of the highest honor.

It is not just ordinary respect. When you respect someone, you think well of them. But when you feel reverence, something more powerful happens: you feel almost small in front of them. There is a sense of being in the presence of something much greater than yourself. You are moved. You are humbled.

Think of it this way: you might respect a good doctor. But you might feel reverence when standing inside an ancient temple, or when meeting a person of extraordinary wisdom, or when you look up at a sky full of stars on a clear night.

Reverence has an inner side and an outer side.

Inner side (the feeling): A deep, quiet, almost sacred kind of admiration. It is calm and serious, not loud or casual. It makes you feel that the thing in front of you deserves to be treated with the greatest care and seriousness.

Outer side (the behavior): Because of this feeling, a person showing reverence tends to speak softly, move carefully, bow their head, or fall silent. They handle things gently. They do not joke around. They treat the person or object as if it deserves to be handled with the utmost care.

For example, a person who enters a place of worship with reverence will walk quietly, avoid disturbance, and behave with solemnity — because the feeling of reverence naturally shapes their behavior.

Reverence can be felt toward many different kinds of things:

  • Religious or spiritual things: God, holy scriptures, sacred places, religious leaders. This is probably the oldest and most common use of the word. Worshippers approach their deity with reverence.
  • Great people: A student might feel reverence for a teacher who changed their life. A historian might speak with reverence about a great leader from the past. Many people feel reverence for their ancestors.
  • Nature: A person standing at the edge of the ocean, looking at a vast mountain range, or watching a solar eclipse might feel a natural sense of reverence — awe mixed with deep respect for something far larger and more powerful than themselves.
  • Ideas and principles: Some people hold truth, justice, or freedom in reverence. When someone treats an idea not just as important but as something almost sacred, that is reverence.
  • Art and knowledge: A musician who feels a deep, almost worshipful admiration for a great composer, or a scientist who approaches their field with the highest seriousness and respect — both are showing a form of reverence.
How reverence differs from similar words

This is important, because reverence is often confused with related words.

Respect vs. reverence: Respect is wide. You can respect many people: a neighbour, a colleague, a stranger who behaves well. Reverence is narrower and far deeper. You reserve it for what you consider truly extraordinary or sacred. All reverence includes respect, but not all respect rises to reverence.

Admiration vs. reverence: Admiration is lighter. You can admire a beautiful painting, a clever move in a chess game, or someone's outfit. Admiration can be casual and brief. Reverence is heavier, more solemn, and more lasting. It carries a quality of the sacred that admiration does not.

Awe vs. reverence: Awe is the feeling of being overwhelmed or stunned by something enormously powerful or impressive — a thunderstorm, a giant waterfall. Awe is about scale and power. Reverence includes awe, but it also includes deep respect and an honoring quality. You revere something not just because it is powerful, but because you consider it worthy of the highest honor. Reverence has a moral and emotional depth that raw awe does not always carry.
How reverence is used in sentences

Seeing the word used in context will make its meaning stick clearly:

  • "She stood before the ancient ruins with reverence, careful not to disturb even a single stone."
  • "He spoke of his grandfather with great reverence, always calling him a man of rare wisdom and honesty."
  • "The congregation bowed their heads in reverence during the prayer."
  • "There was a reverence in the way she turned the pages of that old book — as though each page were a sacred thing."
  • "The soldiers held the flag in reverence, treating it as a symbol of everything their country stood for."

Notice that in each sentence, reverence is not just about liking or respecting something — it is about treating it as something sacred, elevated, and deserving of the most serious honor.

Hold in reverence: To hold something or someone in reverence means to regard them with this deep, solemn respect. "The villagers held the old temple in reverence for centuries."

With reverence: This phrase is used to describe how someone does something — carefully, solemnly, honoring what is in front of them. "She accepted the award with reverence."

Deep reverence: A very common combination. It emphasizes how strong and sincere the feeling is. "He had a deep reverence for all living things."

Reverence for life: A famous phrase, often associated with the idea that life itself — in all its forms — deserves to be treated with the deepest respect. It suggests a worldview in which life is sacred.
The feeling of reverence — described from the inside

Imagine you are visiting a very old library that holds ancient handwritten manuscripts — books that are hundreds of years old. You are allowed into the room where they are kept. Almost automatically, you find yourself speaking in a low voice. You move slowly. You feel a kind of silence settle inside you. You look at the books not with casual curiosity but with a quiet, serious sense that you are in the presence of something extraordinary.

That inner feeling — that combination of deep respect, awe, and the sense that you are in front of something truly worthy of honor — is reverence.

Or imagine meeting someone who, in your view, is a person of extraordinary goodness, wisdom, and character — someone who has lived a life you deeply admire. You are not casual or flippant with them. You choose your words carefully. You listen more than you speak. You feel the weight of their presence. That, too, is reverence.

• Reverence is deeper and more serious than ordinary respect.
  • It carries a solemn, almost sacred quality.
  • It involves both a feeling (inner awe and deep honor) and a behavior (careful, quiet, respectful conduct).
  • It can be directed at religious things, great people, nature, ideas, or anything considered truly worthy of the highest honor.
  • It humbles the person who feels it — you feel small and awed in the presence of what you revere.

If you remember one thing: reverence is what you feel when something strikes you as so truly great, sacred, or worthy that ordinary respect is simply not enough.
